content.text:
I'd choose **candidate 4**, but only with moderate confidence (p ≈ 0.4). I reasoned this out with a continuous approximation of how stock moves under random demand, not by stepping through each day. Candidates 4, 7 and 3 come out within a few dozen units of each other, which is small next to the spread of a single random run.

**Cost of ordering every 2–3 days (candidates 2 and 5).** Each order day costs a fixed 21. Holding one day's demand of both goods costs about 0.6·45 + 0.9·17 ≈ 42 per day. With a fixed cost that small against holding cost, ordering every day is cheapest. Ordering every 2 days saves about 10.5 per day in fixed costs but adds about 21 per day in holding. Ordering every 3 days saves about 14 per day and adds about 42. So candidates 2 and 5 lose to the daily plans.

**Daily plans: how much to order relative to the forecast.** Candidate 7 orders the forecast × 1.048. That is almost exactly the mean demand (forecast × 1.046), so stock neither builds up nor drains on average. The other plans are scaled versions of it:

| Candidate | Order vs. forecast | Order vs. mean demand |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | ×0.95 | about −9 % |
| 7 | ×1.048 | about 0 |
| 6 | ×1.10 | about +5 % |
| 0 | ×1.15 | about +10 % |
| 1 | ×1.25 | about +20 % |

- **The cost of a shortage or a leftover unit:** an unsold unit of demand costs 8 for good 0 and 10 for good 1 (lost margin plus penalty). Stock left at the end costs 4 or 7 per unit (the purchase price). Holding costs 0.6 or 0.9 per unit per day.
- **What happens if you order more than mean demand:** over-ordering doesn't correct itself. With lost sales, stock only gets pulled back up from zero, so with any positive drift it keeps growing. Holding costs then grow roughly with the square of time. Candidates 6, 0 and 1 come out about 180, 540 and more worse than candidate 7.
- **Ordering at the mean versus slightly below:** the best drift is a little below zero, around −1.5 units per day for good 0. Candidate 3 overshoots on good 0 (about 40 worse) and gains a little on good 1 (about 30 better). Overall it is roughly level with candidate 7.

**Candidate 4 versus 7.** The two plans differ only on day 0: candidate 4 orders 68/22 instead of 53/14. That gives an opening buffer of about 15 units of good 0 (on day 4) and 8 of good 1 (on day 3). Both goods start at zero stock at that point, because demand on days 0–3 exceeds the starting stock. For good 0, the buffer cuts expected shortages enough to outweigh the extra purchase and holding, a net gain of about +25. For good 1 the effect is roughly zero.

**Overall ranking:** 4 > 7 ≈ 3 > 6 > 0 > 1, with the batch plans 2 and 5 also clearly behind the top three.

**Pick: candidate 4.** It is candidate 7's plan with a larger first order. Ordering only pays when it heads off shortages, and it adds no holding stock where shortages are already unlikely. All figures below are rough estimates worked out in my head; nothing was simulated.

**What happens in the first days.** All candidates start the same way. Product 0's starting stock of 60 runs out by about day 1, and nothing can arrive before day 4. Product 1's 28 units run out by about day 1 too, with nothing arriving before day 3. So every plan loses sales and pays penalties early, and the first deliveries reach an empty store.

**How the daily plans differ.** These are candidates 0, 1, 3, 4, 6 and 7. Each orders the forecast times a fixed factor. Each pays 27 order fees of 21, about 567 in total.
- **Candidate 7** orders about the average demand (forecast × 1.05). Product 0 orders total 1239 against expected demand of about 1231. Product 1 orders total 483 against about 477. With no surplus building up, shortages still happen through chance (my estimate is about 50 units of product 0 and 18 of product 1). Average stock stays moderate.
- **Candidate 4** adds 15 units of product 0 and 8 of product 1 on day 0. Those units reach an empty store on days 3–4, where a shortage is close to certain. Each extra product 0 unit costs 4 and saves 12 (lost price 9 + penalty 3). Each extra product 1 unit costs 7 and saves 17. They sell within a few days, so holding is small. Net gain over candidate 7 is about +110.
- **Candidates 6, 0 and 1** order 4–19 % more than candidate 7. The surplus builds up over the month (roughly +65, +130 and +245 units of product 0). Holding is expensive: 0.6 per day for a product that costs 4, and 0.9 for one that costs 7. Mid-month, the chance that an extra unit prevents a shortage is under about 50 %, which is worth less than its cost plus holding. My estimate is that candidate 6 is already about 250 worse than candidate 7 on product 0 alone and much worse on product 1. Candidates 0 and 1 are worse still.
- **Candidate 3** orders about 10 % below average demand. That brings large shortage losses, roughly 130 units of product 0 and 60 of product 1. The penalties outweigh the savings on purchases and holding, so it ends up about 280 worse than candidate 7.

**The batch plans.**
- **Candidate 2** orders every other day. It saves about 273 in fees but holds the second day's stock overnight, which costs about 570 extra in holding. It also carries a surplus like candidate 6's. Overall it is worse.
- **Candidate 5** orders every 3 days. It saves about 378 in fees, but stock carried between deliveries costs about 1100 more in holding. Around day 7, product 0's 197-unit delivery plus product 1 already in stock can exceed the 236 capacity, and the excess is lost.

**Handling randomness.** Candidate 4 is also the most robust. Its extra stock goes where a shortage is nearly certain whatever the actual demand turns out to be. After that it tracks average demand, so a big demand shortfall does not leave it with a large pile of stock.

**Candidate 4** has the highest expected profit. I worked it out by hand with a rough random-walk approximation. I didn't simulate step by step on the forecast values, so the gaps between candidates are estimates.

**Batched plans (2 and 5) lose.** Ordering every second or third day saves the 21 daily order fee. But units ordered for later days sit in stock for extra nights. Ordering every 2 days saves 21 per pair of days, while the extra night's storage costs about 45·0.6 + 17·0.9 ≈ 42. Ordering every 3 days saves 42 per three days, while storage costs about 127. Both lose to daily ordering.

**The daily plans differ mainly in how much they order relative to forecast.** Each order arrives L days later, so I compared it with the forecast for its arrival day:
- Candidate 3: about 0.95 of forecast.
- Candidate 7: about 1.05, which matches the average demand multiplier of 1.046. Stock neither builds up nor drains on average.
- Candidate 6: about 1.1 for item 0 and 1.18 for item 1.
- Candidate 0: about 1.15.
- Candidate 1: about 1.25.
- Candidate 4: the same as 7, except the day-0 order is 15 units larger for item 0 and 8 larger for item 1.

**Why ordering above average demand hurts.** The plan is fixed in advance, so any steady excess piles up. For item 0, an extra 5% is about 2.25 units a day. Over the horizon that costs about 234 in extra purchases plus about 400 in extra storage. It saves only about 18 lost sales, worth about 12 each (9 revenue plus 3 penalty). Item 1 behaves the same way. So 6, 0 and 1 are worse than 7, and the gap grows with the excess.

**Why ordering below hurts.** At 0.95 (candidate 3), item 0 runs short by about 125 units. At about 12 per missed unit, that loss outweighs the savings on purchases and storage.

**Why 4 beats 7.** The first deliveries arrive when the shelves are already empty: days 0–3 run short no matter which plan is chosen. Candidate 4's extra day-0 units act as a one-time safety buffer. For item 0 it avoids about 13 lost sales (about +160), against about 60 in purchases and about 35 in storage. For item 1 it gains about 120, against about 56 in purchases and about 36 in storage. That makes 4 roughly 90–100 better than 7 in expectation. The buffer also helps when demand runs above forecast.

**Cash and capacity don't bind.** Cash is lowest around day 4 and stays at several hundred or more, so no order gets cut. Stock stays well under the 236-unit warehouse limit.

**Choice: candidate 4.** I worked this out by hand on the forecast values with rough estimates for the randomness, not an exact simulation.

**What every plan loses in days 0–3.** The first orders arrive on day 4 for item 0 and day 3 for item 1. Until then there is only the starting stock: 60 units of item 0 against about 154 demanded, and 28 units of item 1 against about 48. Every plan therefore runs short and pays penalties at the start, then begins its regular cycle with an empty warehouse.

**Batch plans (2 and 5) cost more than they save.**
- Candidate 2 orders every other day. That saves about 10.5 per day in ordering fees. But half of each batch sits overnight: about 45 units of item 0 at 0.6 and 17 units of item 1 at 0.9, so about 42 per two days, or 21 per day. Holding costs outweigh the fee savings.
- Candidate 5 orders every three days, and its holding costs are higher still: about 127 per three days against 42 saved in fees. On top of that, 197 units of item 0 arrive on day 7 into a 236-unit warehouse, so some of the excess may be lost on arrival.

**Daily plans (0, 1, 3, 4, 6, 7) differ mainly in how far they order above forecast.**
- Candidate 7 orders the forecast times about 1.05, which matches the average demand multiplier. It has no safety stock, and demand swings of about ±13 units of item 0 and ±5 of item 1 per day lead to frequent shortages.
- Candidate 3 orders about 0.95 times the forecast. It is short every day, with a cost of roughly 8 per missing unit of item 0 and 10 per unit of item 1. It is clearly the worst of the daily plans.
- Candidates 6 (about 1.1 for item 0 and 1.2 for item 1), 0 (about 1.15) and 1 (about 1.25) over-order every day. The surplus piles up: candidate 6 buys about 62 extra units of each item over candidate 7. Those units pay holding costs and are largely left unsold at the end, which costs about 4 per unit of item 0 and 7 per unit of item 1. That outweighs the shortages they prevent, and the bigger the over-ordering, the worse the plan.
- Candidate 4 is candidate 7 with a one-time increase on day 0: +15 units of item 0 and +8 of item 1. Because the warehouse starts the cycle empty, this small buffer is very likely to be sold. It covers early shortages without building up surplus. My estimate puts the best buffer at roughly 8–15 units, and this is in that range.

**Under randomness**, candidate 4 holds up best. A one-time buffer protects against demand falling below forecast without wasting stock when demand comes in higher or lower than expected.
